detail.label: achievable
detail.goal: Add a product to the shopping cart.
detail.summary:
Task: Add a product to the shopping cart — SUCCEEDED.

I navigated to the inventory page (already logged in) and clicked "Add to cart" on the Sauce Labs Backpack ($29.99). The action succeeded immediately: the button label changed to "Remove" (confirming the item is now in the cart) and the cart icon counter updated to display "1", giving clear, immediate feedback that the item was added.

What worked well:
1. Clear, unambiguous "Add to cart" button on every product card, requiring no scrolling or hunting.
2. Instant visual feedback — the button toggling to "Remove" makes it obvious the action succeeded and offers an easy way to undo it.
3. The cart item count badge updated immediately in the header, giving a persistent, glanceable confirmation of cart contents without needing to navigate away from the product list.

No usability friction was encountered during this task — the flow was simple and intuitive. No issues to report.

detail.label: achievable
detail.goal: View the items currently in your cart.
detail.summary:
Goal was to view items currently in the cart.

Process: I initially tried to find a "shopping cart" link by its accessible name from the products page, but no such element/name was exposed to accessibility tools (there's only a cart icon in the top-right of the actual page, not labeled in the tree with recognizable text). I had to navigate directly via URL (saucedemo.com/cart.html) to reach the cart page instead of clicking a link.

Result: On the Cart page, the accessibility tree shows "Your Cart", column headers "QTY" and "Description", but no actual line items are listed — the cart is empty. There are no products currently added to the cart. The page offers "Continue Shopping" or "Checkout" as next actions, but no items to review.

Top usability issues found (ranked by impact on completing this goal):
1. Critical/blocking: The cart icon link on the products page is not exposed with any discernible accessible name/text (e.g., "Cart" or "Shopping cart") in the page's accessibility tree — attempts to click by label like "shopping cart link" failed, forcing direct URL navigation as a workaround. Users/assistive tech relying on labeled controls would struggle to locate this critical navigation element.
2. Moderate: The cart page shows headers "QTY" and "Description" but when the cart is empty, there's no explicit message like "Your cart is empty" — this could confuse users into thinking the page failed to load rather than confirming there are simply zero items.
3. Minor: The "Continue Shopping" button contains an icon labeled "Go back" plus text — slightly redundant/inconsistent labeling convention compared to other simple buttons like "Checkout".

What worked well:
1. Direct URL navigation to /cart.html worked instantly and reliably.
2. The cart page layout is clean and simple, with clear "Continue Shopping" and "Checkout" actions.
3. Page load was fast with no performance issues.

Overall: I was able to reach the cart view, but it turned out to be empty (no items were pre-added), and the on-page navigation to the cart was not straightforward via accessible link text, requiring a direct URL as a workaround.

detail.label: achievable
detail.goal: Buy an item: go through checkout to the order-confirmation page.
detail.summary:
Successfully completed the checkout flow on saucedemo.com and reached the order-confirmation page ("Checkout: Complete!"). 

Tasks attempted:
1. Filled in checkout information (First Name: John, Last Name: Doe, Zip: 12345) on checkout-step-one.html and clicked Continue — succeeded, moved to Overview step.
2. Reviewed order overview (item, payment info, shipping info, price breakdown) on checkout-step-two.html and clicked Finish — succeeded.
3. Landed on checkout-complete.html showing "Thank you for your order!" confirmation — goal achieved.

Top usability issues found (ranked by impact on goal):
1. (Minor) The order-confirmation page lacks any order number or purchase summary/total — just a generic thank-you message and image. This makes it hard for a customer to verify or reference exactly what was ordered and for how much after the fact.
2. (Minor) No visible email confirmation notice or next-steps information (e.g., "a confirmation email has been sent to you") on the confirmation page, which would normally reassure the customer.
3. (Minor) The "Generate PDF order" button's purpose/format isn't described — unclear what it will generate or whether it opens a new tab/download, creating slight uncertainty before clicking.

Things that worked well:
1. The checkout process was linear and predictable — each step (Information → Overview → Complete) was clearly labeled with a step indicator ("Checkout: Your Information", "Checkout: Overview", "Checkout: Complete!").
2. The Overview page clearly itemized price breakdown (item total, tax, total) and displayed payment/shipping information concisely before finalizing.
3. The final confirmation message ("Thank you for your order!... arrive just as fast as the pony can get there!") was friendly and had a nice bit of personality/branding (pony express theme), making the completion feel satisfying despite lacking order details.

Overall the checkout flow was quick and frictionless to complete the primary goal, with only minor informational gaps on the confirmation page.

detail.label: achievable
detail.goal: Open the detail page for a specific product.
detail.summary:
Goal accomplished: Successfully navigated to the product detail page for "Sauce Labs Backpack" (https://www.saucedemo.com/inventory-item.html?id=4) by clicking its name/link from the inventory listing page. The detail page correctly displayed the product image, name, full description, price ($29.99), and an "Add to cart" button, along with a "Back to products" navigation link.

Tasks attempted:
1. Open the detail page for a specific product — SUCCEEDED. Clicking the product name link ("Sauce Labs Backpack") on the inventory page took me directly to its dedicated detail page with all expected information.

Top usability issues found:
1. Minor: Each product on the inventory list has TWO separate links (the image link and the text link) both pointing to "#" in the accessibility tree with the same accessible name "Sauce Labs Backpack" — this redundancy could be mildly confusing when tabbing through interactive elements, though it did not block my task since either link led to the same detail page.
2. Minor: The detail page URL uses generic query-string IDs (?id=4) rather than a readable slug, which offers no information in the URL to confirm which product you're viewing at a glance — not a real blocker, but not intuitive either.
3. None encountered that hindered task completion — the flow was straightforward.

Top things that worked well:
1. Clicking the product name from the grid instantly navigated to a clean, focused detail view with matching image, name, description, and price — no ambiguity about product identity.
2. The "Back to products" link/button is clearly labeled and positioned at the top, making it easy to know how to return to the listing.
3. Consistent layout and content between the list and detail views (same description/price) reduced any confusion about whether the correct product was reached.

detail.label: impossible
detail.goal: Apply a discount or coupon code to your order.
detail.summary:
Task: Apply a discount or coupon code to an order on saucedemo.com (Sauce Labs demo store).

What I did:
1. Started at the cart page (cart.html) with one item (Sauce Labs Backpack, $29.99) already in the cart.
2. Searched the cart page for any coupon/promo code field or link — none was present. The cart only showed the item, quantity, description, price, a "Remove" button, "Continue Shopping", and "Checkout" buttons.
3. Proceeded to Checkout, reasoning that a coupon field is commonly located during the checkout information or payment/overview step.
4. On "Checkout: Your Information" step, the only fields shown are First Name, Last Name, and Zip/Postal Code — no coupon or discount code field visible here either.
5. Filled in First Name (Test) and Last Name (User) to continue toward the next step (Overview), where a coupon field might plausibly appear, but ran out of step budget (20/20) before reaching checkout-step-two/overview page to confirm.

Outcome: BLOCKED — I was not able to locate any coupon/discount code entry point on the cart page or the first checkout step, and ran out of allotted steps before reaching the order overview page to check there as well. Based on prior knowledge of this demo site, saucedemo.com does not actually implement a coupon/discount feature at all in its checkout flow, which itself is a significant usability/content gap if a coupon feature is expected by users.

Top 3 usability issues found (ranked by impact on goal):
1. (Critical/Blocking) No coupon or discount code field exists anywhere in the cart or checkout-step-one screens. There is no visible affordance, link, or hint ("Have a promo code?") indicating whether/where a code could be applied, forcing guesswork and step-by-step navigation through checkout with no resolution within the session.
2. (Moderate) The cart page provides no messaging about promotions, discounts, or codes at all — if this is a store that doesn't support coupons, that should be stated, or if it does, the entry point needs to be discoverable from the cart itself (the most natural place a shopper looks first).
3. (Minor) The checkout information step (name/zip) gives no indication of how many steps remain or whether a discount step follows, adding uncertainty about whether continuing forward is the correct path to find a coupon field.

Top 3 things that worked well:
1. Cart page clearly displayed item, quantity, description, and price with a simple, uncluttered layout.
2. Checkout flow navigation (Cart → Checkout: Your Information) was straightforward with clear "Continue"/"Cancel" actions.
3. Form fields on the checkout information step were clearly labeled (First Name, Last Name, Zip/Postal Code) and easy to fill in without ambiguity.

detail.label: impossible
detail.summary:
Goal: View past order history on saucedemo.com (Swag Labs).

Attempted approach: Logged into the site (already on inventory page), opened the hamburger menu ("Open Menu") to look for account/order-related navigation. The menu only exposes four links: "All Items", "About" (external link to saucelabs.com marketing site), "Logout", and "Reset App State". None of these lead to any order history, purchase records, or account/profile page. There is no cart icon badge indicating past orders, and browsing the product inventory page itself offers no historical order data. I also checked footer links (Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn, Terms of Service, Privacy Policy) — none relevant.

Conclusion: This site (a QA testing demo application) does not implement any order history / past purchases feature at all. There is no account dashboard, no "My Orders" section, and no way to view previously placed orders. I was unable to accomplish the goal because the feature simply does not exist anywhere in the site's navigation or pages I could find.

Top usability issues found (ranked by how much they blocked the goal):
1. (Critical) No Order History / My Orders feature exists anywhere on the site — the hamburger menu's four options (All Items, About, Logout, Reset App State) contain no path to past purchase records, completely blocking the task.
2. (Moderate) The "About" link in the main navigation menu takes users to an entirely different external marketing website (saucelabs.com) rather than any account-related page, which could mislead users searching for account/order info into leaving the app.
3. (Minor) There is no account or profile icon/section anywhere in the header or menu, so there's no obvious place a user would even expect order history to live — the app's navigation model doesn't hint that such a feature might exist or where it would be found.

Things that worked well:
1. The hamburger menu opens and closes reliably and clearly labels its four available links.
2. The product inventory page itself is clean, with clear product names, descriptions, and prices, plus a working sort dropdown (Name/Price ascending/descending).
3. Footer navigation (social links, Terms of Service, Privacy Policy) is clearly laid out and consistently present.

Since the feature does not exist, I could not proceed further; ending session as blocked.

detail.label: impossible
detail.goal: Edit your account profile or change your password.
detail.summary:
Goal: Edit account profile or change password on saucedemo.com (Swag Labs).

Attempted: I logged into the site and landed on the inventory/products page. I opened the hamburger "Open Menu" side navigation to look for account/profile settings. The menu only exposed four links: "All Items", "About" (external link to saucelabs.com marketing site), "Logout", and "Reset App State". There was no "Account", "Profile", "Settings", or "Change Password" option anywhere in the navigation, header, or footer. I also checked the footer, which only contained social media links and legal pages (Terms of Service, Privacy Policy) — no account management there either.

Result: FAILED / BLOCKED — the site does not provide any account profile editing or password change functionality. This appears to be a fundamental limitation of the Swag Labs demo application rather than something I overlooked; the app is intentionally a minimal e-commerce demo/testing sandbox with login, product browsing, cart, and checkout flows only.

Top usability issues found (ranked by how much they blocked my goal):
1. (Serious) No account/profile management feature exists at all — no way to edit profile details or change password from any visible entry point (side menu, header, footer). This completely blocks the task with no workaround or guidance.
2. (Minor) The side menu briefly had a z-index/overlay glitch during my first attempt to click a product link — the closed menu's nav elements intercepted pointer events, requiring an explicit "Close Menu" click to fully dismiss it. This is a minor interaction friction, not related to my main goal but worth flagging.
3. (Minor) There is no in-app help, FAQ, or account-support link that might have pointed me to why account editing isn't available or where to go for such changes (e.g., no "Contact support" link), leaving the dead end with no clarifying content.

Top things that worked well:
1. The hamburger menu is simple, clearly labeled with an "Open Menu"/"Close Menu" icon pair, and easy to discover.
2. Navigation labels (Logout, Reset App State, About) are unambiguous in their intended function, even though they don't include what I needed.
3. Page load and interactions elsewhere were fast and responsive, with no broken links among the available menu items.

detail.label: impossible
detail.goal: Save an item to a wishlist for later.
detail.summary:
Task: Save an item to a wishlist for later. Result: FAILED/BLOCKED - no wishlist feature exists on this site.

I explored the Swag Labs (saucedemo.com) demo store thoroughly:
1. Reviewed the product listing page (inventory.html) with all 6 products.
2. Checked the hamburger navigation menu, which only contains: "All Items", "About" (external link to saucelabs.com), "Logout", and "Reset App State" — no wishlist or favorites option.
3. Clicked into an individual product detail page (Sauce Labs Backpack) to check if a wishlist/save action was available there instead of on the listing page.
4. In both the listing and detail views, the only interactive action per product is "Add to cart" — there is no heart icon, "Save for later," "Add to wishlist," or any equivalent affordance anywhere in the UI.

Since the site provides no wishlist mechanism at all, I could not accomplish the goal of saving an item to a wishlist. This is a fundamental feature gap rather than a discoverability problem — I searched the primary navigation, the product grid, and the product detail page without finding any hint of such functionality.

Top usability issues (ranked by impact on this goal):
1. (Critical) No wishlist/save-for-later feature exists anywhere in the app — this completely blocks the task in scope.
2. (Moderate) The navigation menu is very minimal, offering no hint of other planned functionality (like wishlists) even as a "coming soon" placeholder, which could otherwise reduce user confusion about whether the feature exists.
3. (Minor) "Add to cart" is the only call-to-action per product, which could mislead users who want to bookmark an item without committing to purchase it — there's no lower-commitment way to mark interest in a product.

Things that worked well:
1. Product listing and sorting (Name A-Z, Z-A, Price low-high, high-low) worked clearly and was easy to understand.
2. Navigating from product list to product detail page and back ("Back to products") was smooth and intuitive.
3. Page structure and labeling of buttons (e.g., "Add to cart") was clear and consistent across list and detail views.

detail.label: impossible
detail.goal: Track the shipping status of an order.
detail.summary:
Task: Track the shipping status of an order on saucedemo.com.

Result: Blocked / Not achievable. After logging in with the standard_user demo credentials, I explored the full site structure available to a logged-in user: the product inventory page, the hamburger menu (All Items, About, Logout, Reset App State), and the footer. There is no account/profile area, no order history page, and no "track order" or shipping status feature anywhere in the navigation or footer. The site's functionality is limited to browsing products, adding items to a cart, and (presumably) a checkout flow — it has no concept of past orders or shipment tracking at all. I could not proceed further toward the goal because the feature simply does not exist on this site.

Top usability issues found (ranked by impact on my goal):
1. (Critical) No order tracking or shipping status feature exists anywhere in the app — no order history, no account section, no "track order" link. This completely blocks the task with no workaround.
2. (Moderate) The hamburger menu options (All Items, About, Logout, Reset App State) give no indication of where account/order-related information might live, so a user has to check every menu item and the footer before concluding the feature is absent — wasted effort with no feedback.
3. (Minor) The "About" link exits the demo site entirely to saucelabs.com marketing page, which is a distraction when looking for account/order functionality — it's not clearly labeled as an external company site link.

Things that worked well:
1. Login flow was fast, and the login page itself is helpful — it pre-fills/documents valid demo usernames and the shared password directly on the page, so authentication was frictionless.
2. The product inventory page loaded quickly and clearly displays product names, images, descriptions, and prices in a clean, readable grid layout.
3. The hamburger menu is simple and discoverable, and clearly indicates all top-level navigation options available in the app (even though none relate to order tracking).
